speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) what criteria distinguishes a severe noise dispute qualifying for Community Relations Unit intervention; and (b) given that the one-year pilot in Tampines handled only five severe cases while not deploying noise sensors, what is the Ministry’s assessment of (i) the unit’s efficacy and (ii) whether its enforcement powers are operationally useful.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is neither desirable for our community spirit nor sustainable for Government to step in as a first response for all disputes between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Community Relations Unit (CRU) framework strikes a balance between Government stepping in to manage a dispute and leaving enough room for neighbours to settle disputes themselves.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is not a panacea for neighbour disputes and it is not a substitute for a strong foundation of positive community norms, good neighbourly relations and community dispute resolution options.
CRU has a range of investigatory and enforcement powers, including the power to install noise sensors.
These noise sensors are used as a confirmatory tool, after CRU's initial investigations narrow down from which unit the noise nuisance might be coming from.
The CRU framework is a useful step forward but its implementation requires significant amounts of resources.
Therefore, it is piloted in one town first, Tampines, focusing on severe neighbour noise and hoarding cases.
We are reviewing this pilot carefully, to ensure our systems and processes are effective and we have resourced it correctly and sustainably before we extend the CRU services to other towns.

As Minister Edwin Tong and the Senior Minister of State Sim Ann explained in their Second Reading speeches in November 2024, CRU focuses on severe cases that frontline agencies, like the Housing and Development Board (HDB) and the Police, triage and escalate to it.
These cases represent a small proportion of all disputes between neighbours.

They can include cases where one neighbour is deliberately making excessive noise at unreasonable hours and/or over prolonged periods to cause suffering to surrounding neighbours and where prior mediation has not been successful.
Severe cases with a mental health nexus are another example.
The one case involving deliberate use of noise to disturb neighbours and not related to mental health has abated after joint intervention by CRU, the Police and the Town Council.
CRU will continue to take on severe cases in Tampines that frontline agencies escalate to it.
As a deterrent and a last resort after exhausting all levers, CRU may refer the most severe and recalcitrant nuisance-makers to HDB, to consider compulsory acquisition of their flats.
We will take this course of action only after due care and careful consideration.
This has reduced inter-floor noise transmission by up to five decibels.
For existing flats, the scope for major infrastructure changes is limited.
Nevertheless, residents can practise simple steps to reduce inter-floor noise.
They can for example, place rubber padding or "chair socks" on the legs of furniture.
HDB will also continue to explore other possible solutions through research and development.
HDB does not otherwise track the number of disputes between neighbours in HDB flats, or the number of cases that escalated into physical altercations.
Ultimately, we need strong community bonds and strong community norms, so fewer disputes will arise.
And where they do arise, parties involved are more likely to resolve their differences in an amicable and mutually acceptable manner, if these norms and practices are strong.
This is an outcome worth working towards as a "we first" society.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have three supplementary questions for the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) and two supplementary questions for the Ministry of National Development (MND).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For the MinLaw, I would respectfully disagree with the Ministry's view.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Because for most of the residents who have appealed for compulsory mediation, and I have written two letters through the Member of Parliament (MP), generally, would the Senior Minister of State not agree that the MP is a sufficient gatekeeper of these compulsory mediation appeals to the Ministry?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, for residents outside of Tampines, how should they currently appeal for compulsory mediation?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Should they appeal to HDB to come down to their units to see their circumstances for themselves?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And I quote a Mothership article of 2024, which reported a Bukit Panjang resident who got a CDRT injunction for their neighbour to stop smoking in June 2023, but found it, subsequently, difficult to get the evidence to get an enforcement order when her neighbour persisted in smoking.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, less than 1% of them have been deemed severe.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second supplementary question, if no sensors were deployed, what unique capability did CRU add beyond current procedures by HDB and the Police, which already mediate and investigate?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I mentioned in my speech just now that Mr Tiong asked for the number of compulsory mediations for neighbour disputes at CMC for each of the last five years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, with that clarification, let me now deal with the supplementary questions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The first point about whether the MP can be the gatekeeper.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: My response is to point out that as far as the issue of directing compulsory mediation is concerned, that has to be dealt with even-handedly and also, it involves two institutions: one, the judge, which is an independent branch of our Government; and the other one, is in relation to the public officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, we sited it with the public officers as far as compulsory mediation is concerned, so that anybody who is aggrieved, he may write or his MP may write to the public body concerned and then, they will look at it and see whether or not there is a need to issue a Mediation Direction (MD).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Because when the MPs get information, they only hear one side of the story.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is very difficult to hear both sides of the story.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But the public officers are able to do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the judiciary level, as I mentioned my speech, the judges have discretion to order mediation as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, cumulatively, we are able to deal with this matter, ensuring that mediation is really the main thrust of our approach or strategy to deal with neighbours' disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member asked about compulsory mediation outside the Tampines project.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I certainly remember the debate that happened in the last session of Parliament, where almost every Member asked that his constituency be volunteered for the extension after the pilot.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I come to the last supplementary question, which is an assertion that the CDRT is toothless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am just looking at it from the perspective of the legislative framework.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, there have been instances where respondents have been ordered to leave their homes for a period of 10 days and 14 days.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, these measures are certainly measures with serious outcomes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think there are two parts to it: one is with regard to the efficacy of CRU and the expansion; and the second is whether CRU has special powers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In this regard, Sir, I would also like to ask the Member if he can 100% guarantee that any of these suite of measures, including the CRU, can de-escalate a neighbour dispute, and then I will respond shortly.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Clearly, I think we cannot 100% guarantee de-escalation, but it will make sense at the margins.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Regardless of whatever we do, there is no 100% guarantee.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: You apply CDRT, CMC, or even to that regard, CRU, to any of these cases, it can help, it can also hinder, and in certain cases as well, it may even exacerbate the situation.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, there is no special power that CRU has and so, let us exercise reason.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Let us exercise reason to it and recognise that there is no tool that is perfect and recognise that we have a useful suite of tools that are available to us, thanks to the enhanced CDMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we are using those tools and we are using novel tools in the Tampines pilot with regard to the CRU as well as the MD, but there is no perfect tool in this regard.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But what CRU does is help to be an intermediary, between voluntary mediation as well as enforcement.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And that is what it is purporting to do.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the November 2024 Second Reading, I think, many Members of this House, from across both aisles, have naturally asked for the expansion of CRU beyond the Tampines pilot.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I understand that and I am no exception.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In fact, I think that was one of the biggest asks across.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: At this point, I also wanted to remind Members in the Second Reading last year that Ms Sylvia Lim had also asked for the expansion of the CRU pilot, amongst many other Members in this House.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But what is also very useful is that Members of this House also acknowledged two things.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: One, is that this is a multi-year effort by several Ministries and agencies, and I thank Members for duly acknowledging that.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But the more important point is that Ms Sylvia Lim, while asking like many Members to expand the CRU pilot, she had also acknowledged the resource-intensive and challenging nature of the work.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I quote Ms Lim, she said, "It is also clear that the enhanced CDMF will be a resource-intensive exercise requiring standby teams after office hours and active management of difficult cases by the new Director-General of Community Relations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The work will not be easy." And I thought this is just useful for us.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are working very hard on learning from the five cases that we have in Tampines.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I have given, in my reply, the outcomes of these CRU cases in Tampines.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we are also looking at cases outside of Tampines, that some Members have also floated to us.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One, as noise disturbances and hoarding in common areas remain among the most frequent neighbour disputes in HDB estates, would the Ministry consider reviewing and strengthening legislation and enforcement, including setting maximum permissible decibel levels or clearer hoarding thresholds, to address these issues more proactively?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two, has the Ministry explore the use of predictive analytics or risk assessment tools to identify the high-risk neighbour disputes before they escalate?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And three, if so, what safeguards are in place to ensure there is fairness, transparency and privacy?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She suggested whether the legislation can be reviewed further, to put specific noise levels.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Certainly, that is something that we can consider.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would give her and hon Members an assurance that we are continually looking to see how we can strengthen the system, because we know how important this issue about ensuring neighbourliness and harmony in the community is.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But I think one must agree, the core point is that these issues must be dealt with in the community and the community must exercise self-moderation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We should not be directing cases to be dealt with at the CDRT as a first resort.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also wanted to assure Members and in fact, last year at the Second Reading, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann had also assured Members, that there will be safeguards to protect residents' privacy in the deployment of noise sensors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We are studying these, the way in which the CRU is managing these cases.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And we see that there are some encouraging signs, but please just do give us some time to study this in detail – and also, cases outside of the pilot – so that we can better think about resourcing it.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think we discussed this in detail last year and I really ask for Members' patience in this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Work with us, we are serious about this, we are working hard on this and we will take all of the learnings very seriously, and your feedback into account.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To improve the process, I wanted to ask whether the Ministry is studying ways to further simplify or digitise the evidence submission process for CDRT hearings, to make it more accessible for laypersons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I mentioned in my speech, there is a website which provides very important information on how to collate evidence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And also, I would say the CRU has been formed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The legislative intent is also to assist applicants in certain cases by gathering evidence and that can be presented to the CDRT.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Or in a very clear cut case, the CRU itself can issue abatement orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, collectively, this will assist the neighbour who is belabouring under some disamenities from his other neighbour.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: According to what I know from The Straits Times, 90% of neighbourly disputes are actually resolved at the grassroots level.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: They often work late into the night on their own time to preserve the harmony between neighbours and the community.

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: How can we enhance the ecosystem of support, including resources, so that our grassroots mediators can do their job and play this vital role, before formal escalation to the suite of measures that had been mentioned?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: And most importantly, given the anxiety over the murder in Yishun, how can we enhance the safety of our grassroots leaders so that they can do this work with peace of mind as they work deep into the night?

speaker: Mr Ng Chee Meng (Jalan Kayu)
text: Perhaps training for some pick-up of warning signs and maybe techniques to de-escalate more serious scenarios?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They do it on their own time, dealing with disputes involving neighbours.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And also, they take their own time to train themselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And as a result of which, a substantial number of neighbour disputes are being solved through them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would add, Sir, that, actually, there is also another aspect of what they do, which is really creating the goodwill through community activities, getting the neighbours to meet one another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is something that we took for granted during the kampung days when our doors were always open.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Here, the grassroots leaders come, make sure that neighbours meet one another through, say, block parties and other events for residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And that is very helpful because with the relationship that is built, the neighbour who is originally thinking of complaining, may say, "Eh, wait a minute, I know his circumstances, I know his family well, maybe I will live with it".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And that is the live-and-let-live attitude that we want to promote in the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mediation is not an easy area for many of them because they may not be legally trained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, we are certainly happy to see how we can train more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, at the CMC level, we are also looking out for suitable candidates to increase our core of mediators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We can certainly continue to share best practices and that is one way to strengthen the competence of our grassroots leaders as mediators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the issue of the anxiety following the incident in Yishun, I would say this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mediation is not suitable when there are signs of violence, threatened or actual.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: You should break off and then let the Police deal with it and that must be something ingrained in everybody's mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And of course, sometimes we are dealing with evolving situations and there must be a constant assessment as to whether the line is crossed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Even last night, I was also dealing with one case and my volunteer stayed late night, and I think many of us can attest to that as well.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, this is a shout out to many of the volunteers who work very hard to mediate and also to build the community bonds that are very important upstream.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If I may also just to suggest that Members, please continue to support the Municipal Services Office's (MSO's) ongoing work in this front.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MSO has a Love Our 'Hood Youth Challenge, as well as HDB's Singapore's Friendly Neighbourhood Award.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are just some measures in which we can take all of these upstream.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I just wanted to also reflect that these upstream measures are complemented by what Senior Minister of State Murali and I had outlined today, a comprehensive suite of measures for the enhanced CDMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: They are not panaceas, but taken together, I think we can build that "we-first" society that we all aspire to.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Although you did not file a Parliamentary Question, since your name was quoted by Minister of State Tan, I will give you the floor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister of State of MND.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier on, when he said that the CRU officers do not have special powers, I just wanted to understand what he meant by that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For example, they can issue orders on the spot and so on, so I wonder whether he could clarify that point, what he meant by CRU officers do not have special powers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe I was wrong on that point, because it was later clarified that the CRU does not work after office hours, so I would like him to clarify that on that point.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I think it was the Member Kenneth Tiong's term, special powers or super powers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, the Member is absolutely right, there are a few.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think in the Second Reading, it had already been mentioned under different sections: in section 13E, under section 13M.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These are powers that the CRU have been afforded under the Bill which was passed last year.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I just wanted to clarify because I did not say special powers and that is why I wanted to make sure that it is very clear.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That is why I asked the Member Kenneth Tiong about what he really meant by special powers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If he meant that it would be a special antidote or panacea to resolving this, then it is not.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think we have agreed that the CRU would not be able to do that.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: That any intervention could help, it could also hinder.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I think just to clarify that exchange between me and Member Kenneth Tiong, that is what I meant.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But Ms Lim is spot on, that there are powers afforded to the CRU as outlined by the Second Reading last year.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have two supplementary questions related to a particular step, which is the service and enforcement step of the process.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: You gave a lot of data on the number of cases, the number of resolutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I actually wanted to clarify if you had mentioned, maybe I missed it, was there data on the proportion or number of CDRT cases that are actually enforced?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, that is my first supplementary question, and I ask that because I hear from the ground that actually, that percentage can be fairly low.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And my second supplementary question related to that is under the current framework.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I understand that the affected neighbour who initiated the CDRT is actually the one that is responsible for service and enforcement of the orders from CDRT and that would involve either going through the process server, or, as you said earlier, to make an application to the court.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These, of course, can be quite intimidating to the average resident.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, my question is, will the Government consider shifting the responsibility for service of CDRT orders to a Government agency, and related to that, are CRU orders treated the same way?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Do those also have to be served and enforced by the affected neighbours?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I take the hon Member's points and we will convey her feedback to the Judiciary as to the modes of service of CDRT orders that should be available to the successful litigant after the CDRT hearing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Insofar as CRU orders are concerned, that is dealt with by the unit itself, so, that should not present an issue.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And certainly, the framework is really to assist the resident.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Because the CRU, through the enhanced legislative framework, is able to make the investigations and in a clear cut case, issue an abatement order.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And thereafter, if it is not complied with, then, it can escalate and consider enforcement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I mentioned just now, in response to the hon Member Mr Kenneth Tiong, there could be eviction orders and pursuant to which the person has to leave his house, or there could also be compulsory acquisition by HDB.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, these are all the measures that are available.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Okay, there are still many Members who wish to ask questions, so please keep your supplementary question as short as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Taking these points, I would like to make a suggestion to MND, which I had actually raised in a previous Sitting five years ago, and that is a very simple solution for MND to set threshold levels on noise, educate the public on it and then take enforcement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would respectfully suggest this solves several issues: it avoids the entire sway, the resources needed to decide each noise case, case-by-case in mediation, and then CDRU and then everywhere else.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Instead, with a clear benchmark and enforcement, the first point of contact for most people is to call the Police.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are guidelines, they can enforce, or a suitable MND officer can enforce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful for MND's consideration on this.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I asked this in my original Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And if the CRU which has greater expertise in handling neighbour disputes, if it never gets referred cases, how would it be able to achieve any significant success?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, for the Senior Minister of State for Law, can he confirm that the plans are for grassroots leaders or grassroots advisers to issue mandatory mediation orders?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because if it is grassroots advisers, then I believe all, but 10 of the grassroots advisers in Singapore are also MPs, which will present the same problems as the Senior Minister of State mentioned in his response to Mr Kenneth Tiong.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Please let me get back to the Member on those numbers.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The Member mentioned earlier on about whether we could have expanded it and what are the measures that we can take?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Can the Member just repeat his question, please?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am referring to the expansion within a town.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, Tampines town had six months to run this pilot, but it is taken on only five cases so far.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Is this the rate of referrals that we can expect moving forward, when it is expanded to other towns?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I think, it is, I mean, inherent in that question is also a very important question that we want to ask.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: How many referral cases do we want to have and how many serious cases we want to have?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think, the Member would agree with me that we would ideally have less cases.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I mean, you would because at the upstream you would have addressed them – but let me respond to this.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The fact is that we are looking at all of these five cases.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We have seen some encouraging signs within all of these different five cases that the CRU has already addressed and we are studying these very carefully for us to see what we can do.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also want to take this opportunity to say that the CRU officers – I mean earlier on, the Member Kenneth Tiong, also mentioned that you have how many different officers, and then why are there just five cases?

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: My officers at the CRU have worked very hard on these cases.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And as the Member would appreciate, these are very complicated cases and that is exactly why these are severe cases that have been referred to by HDB and the Police.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: If they are normal cases that are easily managed in the community or in CMC or other measures, then they would not have been.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I wanted to just make the point that ideally, we would address many of these cases upstream, but where there are severe cases downstream, that is where the pilot has shown us some ways to deal with it, in concert with and augmented by, the suite of CDMF measures that are already there.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I really wanted to thank my public officers, because in this regard, they have worked incredibly hard and spent incredible amount of time in the five cases in Tampines.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I have mentioned to them that we are open to taking on even more cases, severe cases, to be precise, that have been escalated to us by Police and HDB.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: One supplementary question for the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Understand there are considerations to extend the CRU framework beyond Tampines to other towns, if the pilot is successful.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The constant distress caused by noise transmission is a root cause of many disputes that escalate, including pickleball.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am glad to hear that new BTO developments now feature increased floor slab thickness.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For the first one, on the mandatory logging and tracking system, and then the second one on the subsidised soundproofing.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These require, again, resources, as well as careful learning.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And I think pilots, even beyond Tampines, we will look into these and then, if relevant or appropriate, we will consider them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My supplementary question is directed to MinLaw and it is about inter-agency coordination.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When neighbour disputes turn violent, how do we better capture the warning signs, such as, repeated Police calls, past mediation cases, Town Council's complaints?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And can the Ministry work with the Police, HDB, Town Council and MOH, perhaps to set up an early warning system so that when multiple reports come in from various agencies about the same household, agencies can act decisively before tensions boil over?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And is the current data sharing between CMC, CDRT, the Singapore Police Force really robust enough to flag dangers early?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Certainly, I am aware that there is a level of cooperation between the agencies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think he is looking towards a proper framework so that we can better detect cases which may become violent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is certainly something that we can consider.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: First of all, I would like to thank the HDB officers for all their help.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I think they have been putting in a lot of effort to help resolve some of these dispute cases.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And I am very thankful that HDB has also chosen Tampines to pilot the CRU.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I just have one question for MND's consideration.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I think a lot of the focus has been on the mental health of the neighbours that have potentially been causing a lot of these nuisances.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But I also have cases where the mental health of the neighbours on the receiving end have been very badly affected.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And I wonder if this could be a consideration, in terms of the severity criteria for MND to step in and activate CRU.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I mentioned earlier on some of the criteria that we had and how the CRU takes on some of these cases.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also mentioned earlier on about severe cases with regard to a mental health nexus, as well as prolonged and unreasonable interference.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: There are also in the Second Reading, some details about what criteria we are looking at.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But as I mentioned earlier on, let us look at the cases, let us study the pilot which is, again, only six months old, and then, take in your feedback and apply as appropriate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I also wanted to get back to Member Gerald Giam on his question about Tampines.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Speaker, I just have a question for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I heard in his reply that MinLaw is planning to work with HDB and MND to refer more cases for directed mediation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, if the Senior Minister of State could share in more concrete detail how the Ministry plans to get more cases referred for directed mediation, because I do agree with the Senior Minister of State that this must be one of the centres of gravity for the CDMF framework going forward.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The idea, and I would take the opportunity to reiterate our framework, is to settle the bulk of disputes in the community itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is really using the resources that the hon Member Mr Ng Chee Meng said – our grassroots leaders and community leaders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, that is the bulwark of the cases that we would have to deal with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Beyond that, there needs to be an assessment made by the public officers, HDB and CRU, to see whether or not these are the cases where it may make sense for the issuance of the formal MD.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, again, one has to look at the context.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In a situation where the CRU is of the view that the case is made out straightaway, it is a straightforward case made out, it may not even bother the residents to go for mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, that is not necessary for them to go through the entire process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And in situations where they feel that there are no troublesome signs like threats of violence and all that, that is the situation where the legislative policy contemplates the issuance of the MD.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And I guess as we gather more experience from the pilot, we will finetune the protocols and make sure that the aim behind this CDMF, which is really to ensure that our community self-moderates when it comes to the dealing of disputes, ensures that as far as possible, we do not invoke the formal processes, which also includes MD, so that neighbours not only can live and let live, but also continue on in the spirit that we would want to see.
